title: Mathematics 2
target_note: 27 questions in 40 minutes. A-level content, and almost every question has a standard method that will not fit in ninety seconds alongside a shorter one that will.

questions.stem_html: Simplify √12 + √27√3.
questions.solution_html:
√12 = 2√3 and √27 = 3√3, so the top is 5√3.

Dividing by √3 leaves 5.

Simplify the surds before dividing and the √3 cancels outright. Rationalising the denominator first works and wastes thirty seconds.

traps.A: The result of dividing only one term.
traps.B: √27/√3 alone, forgetting √12/√3 = 2.
traps.C: The numerator's second term, undivided.
traps.E: The numerator, with the division not carried out.
traps.F: 12 + 27 = 39, then √39 mis-simplified — the surds were added inside the root.

questions.stem_html: Work out 82/3 × 16−1/4.
questions.solution_html:
82/3 = (√83)2 = 22 = 4, and 16−1/4 = 1161/4 = 12.

4 × 12 = 2.

The negative index inverts; it does not make the answer negative. Taking the root before the power keeps every number small.

traps.A: Only the second factor.
traps.C: Only the first factor — the 16 term dropped.
traps.D: 8^(2/3) read as 8^2 ÷ 3, or the indices added.
traps.E: 4 × 4 — the negative index ignored.
traps.F: 4 × 8, from misreading both indices.

questions.stem_html: Solve log2 x + log2(x − 6) = 4.
questions.solution_html:
Combine: log2(x(x−6)) = 4, so x2 − 6x = 16.

x2 − 6x − 16 = 0 factorises as (x−8)(x+2) = 0.

x = −2 makes both logarithms undefined, so the only solution is 8.

The quadratic has two roots and the question has one answer. Option F exists for anyone who solves correctly and forgets that a logarithm needs a positive argument.

traps.A: A root of the quadratic, but log₂(−2) is undefined.
traps.D: log₂(0) is undefined.
traps.F: −2 must be rejected: the logarithms are undefined there.

questions.detail: A log equation with a rejected root

questions.stem_html:
Solve 22x − 5 × 2x + 4 = 0.

What is the sum of the solutions?
questions.solution_html:
22x = (2x)2, so with t = 2x this is t2 − 5t + 4 = 0.

(t−1)(t−4) = 0 gives t = 1 or 4, so x = 0 or x = 2.

Sum 2.

x = 0 is easy to discard as 'no solution'. 20 = 1 is perfectly valid and it is half the answer.

traps.A: One of the two solutions, not their sum.
traps.B: A value of t, not of x.
traps.D: The other value of t.
traps.E: The sum of the two values of t.
traps.F: There are two.

questions.stem_html:
The curve y = 3x is reflected in the y-axis.

What is the y-coordinate of the image curve when x = 2?
questions.solution_html:
Reflecting in the y-axis replaces x by −x, giving y = 3−x.

At x = 2: 3−2 = 19.

Reflection in the y-axis changes the sign of x; reflection in the x-axis changes the sign of y and would give −9.

traps.B: 1/(3 × 2) — the index treated as a multiplier.
traps.C: 3^(−1), reading the reflection as a shift of one.
traps.D: 3^1 — the reflection applied to the wrong variable.
traps.E: 3 × 2, not 3 to a power.
traps.F: 3² — the original curve, unreflected.

questions.stem_html:
The equation x2 − (k+1)x + k = 0 has two roots that differ by 3.

What is the sum of the possible values of k?
questions.solution_html:
The equation factorises for every k: (x−1)(x−k) = 0, so the roots are 1 and k.

They differ by 3 when |k − 1| = 3, giving k = 4 or k = −2.

Sum 2.

Spotting that x = 1 is always a root removes the discriminant entirely. Going via (x₁−x₂)2 = (k+1)2 − 4k reaches the same place through far more algebra.

traps.A: The product of the two values of k.
traps.B: One of the two values.
traps.C: Assuming the values are symmetric about zero; they are symmetric about 1.
traps.E: The other value.
traps.F: 4 + 2, with the sign of −2 lost.

questions.detail: Roots that differ by a fixed amount

questions.stem_html: How many integers x satisfy x2 − 5x + 6 < 0?
questions.solution_html:
(x−2)(x−3) < 0 holds exactly for 2 < x < 3.

There is no integer strictly between 2 and 3, so the answer is 0.

The roots 2 and 3 are integers, which makes it feel as though they should count. The inequality is strict, and they are the endpoints, not the interior.

traps.B: There is no integer strictly between 2 and 3.
traps.C: Counting the roots 2 and 3, which do not satisfy a strict inequality.
traps.D: Counting 2, 3 and one more.
traps.E: Counting every integer from −1 to 3, ignoring the inequality.
traps.F: The solution set is an interval of length 1 containing no integers.

questions.detail: A quadratic inequality with no integers

questions.stem_html:
p(x) = 2x3 + ax2 − 5x + b has (x − 1) as a factor, and leaves remainder 12 when divided by (x − 2).

What is ab?
questions.solution_html:
p(1) = 0: 2 + a − 5 + b = 0, so a + b = 3.

p(2) = 12: 16 + 4a − 10 + b = 12, so 4a + b = 6.

Subtracting: 3a = 3, so a = 1 and b = 2, giving ab = 2.

Two substitutions and one subtraction. Long division of the cubic by both linear factors gets there and costs three minutes.

traps.A: Sign error in one of the substitutions.
traps.C: a + b, not ab.
traps.D: The right-hand side of the second equation.
traps.E: A slip solving the simultaneous equations.
traps.F: The remainder, not the product.

questions.stem_html:
f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x2.

How many real solutions does fg(x) = gf(x) have?
questions.solution_html:
fg(x) = 2x2 + 1 and gf(x) = (2x+1)2 = 4x2 + 4x + 1.

Setting them equal: 2x2 + 4x = 0, so 2x(x+2) = 0 and x = 0 or −2 — 2 solutions.

The constant 1 cancels from both sides, which is what keeps this to a two-line question. Expanding and then solving a general quadratic is the slow route.

traps.A: The equation does have solutions; x = 0 is one.
traps.B: x = 0 is easy to lose by dividing through by x.
traps.D: The resulting equation is a quadratic, so at most two.
traps.E: Both composites are quadratics, but their difference is not quartic.
traps.F: The two composites are different functions.

questions.stem_html:
u1 = 2 and un+1 = 3un − 2.

What is u6?
questions.solution_html:
2, 4, 10, 28, 82, 244.

Each term is 3 times the last, less 2. Five steps is quicker than finding the closed form — though it is un = 3n−1 + 1 if you want to check.

Six terms means five applications of the rule, not six. Stopping at 82 is the commonest way to lose this.

traps.A: The fourth term.
traps.B: The fifth term — one step short.
traps.C: An arithmetic slip at the last step.
traps.D: Multiplying by 3 and subtracting 2 in the wrong order somewhere.
traps.E: 3⁵ − 1 rather than 3⁵ + 1.

questions.stem_html:
The sum of the first n terms of a series is Sn = 3n2 + 2n.

What is the tenth term?
questions.solution_html:
The nth term is Sn − Sn−1.

S10 = 320 and S9 = 261, so the tenth term is 59.

The series is arithmetic with first term 5 and common difference 6, so the tenth term is 5 + 9(6) = 59 as well. Either route is quick; computing all ten terms is not.

traps.A: S₂ − S₁, the second term.
traps.B: S₁₀ ÷ 10, the mean term.
traps.C: A slip in S₉.
traps.D: The ninth term.
traps.F: S₁₀ itself — the sum, not the term.

questions.detail: A term from a sum formula

questions.stem_html:
A geometric series has first term 8 and sum to infinity 12.

What is its third term?
questions.solution_html:
S∞ = a1 − r, so 12 = 81 − r and r = 13.

Third term = 8r2 = 8 × 19 = 89.

The third term uses r2, not r. Option D is the second term and is the one most often chosen.

traps.A: Half the third term, or 8r² with r = 1/6.
traps.C: 8r with r mis-solved.
traps.D: The second term, 8r.
traps.E: 12 − 8, the remaining sum rather than a term.
traps.F: Twice the second term.

questions.detail: Third term of a convergent series

questions.stem_html: What is the coefficient of x3 in the expansion of (1 + 2x)5(1 − x)?
questions.solution_html:
(1 + 2x)5 has x2 coefficient 5C2 × 4 = 40 and x3 coefficient 5C3 × 8 = 80.

Multiplying by (1 − x): the x3 term is 80 × 1 + 40 × (−1) = 40.

Only two terms of the binomial matter. Expanding all six and then multiplying out is the long way round.

traps.A: ⁵C₃ × 2 — the 2 not cubed.
traps.B: An arithmetic slip in ⁵C₃ × 8.
traps.D: 80 − 20, using the wrong lower coefficient.
traps.E: The x³ coefficient of the binomial alone, forgetting the (1 − x).
traps.F: 80 + 40 — the minus sign lost.

questions.stem_html: What is the y-intercept of the perpendicular bisector of the line segment joining (1, 2) and (5, 8)?
questions.solution_html:
Midpoint (3, 5). The segment has gradient 64 = 32, so the bisector has gradient −23.

y − 5 = −23(x − 3). At x = 0: y = 5 + 2 = 7.

Two things have to be right at once: the midpoint and the negative reciprocal. Getting the gradient as −32 instead gives 9.

traps.A: The x-coordinate of the midpoint.
traps.B: The y-coordinate of the midpoint — the intercept of a horizontal line through it.
traps.C: A slip substituting x = 0.
traps.D: Using gradient −1/3.
traps.F: Using gradient −3/2, the negative rather than the negative reciprocal.

questions.stem_html:
A chord of length 8 is drawn in a circle of radius 5.

How far is the chord from the centre?
questions.solution_html:
The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, giving a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 5 and one leg 4.

The distance is √25 − 16 = 3.

Half the chord is 4, not 8. Using the full chord gives √25−64, which is not real — a useful sign you have gone wrong.

traps.A: Half of the correct answer.
traps.C: √(25 − 14), an arithmetic slip.
traps.D: Half the chord, not the distance.
traps.E: √(25 + 16) — added instead of subtracted.
traps.F: 25 − 16 without taking the root.

questions.detail: Chord to distance from the centre

questions.stem_html:
The point (5, 7) lies on the circle (x − 2)2 + (y − 3)2 = 25.

What is the gradient of the tangent there?
questions.solution_html:
The centre is (2, 3), so the radius to (5, 7) has gradient 7 − 35 − 2 = 43.

The tangent is perpendicular to the radius, so its gradient is −34.

No differentiation needed — the radius does all the work. Implicit differentiation gets the same answer in four times the space.

traps.A: The negative of the radius gradient, not its negative reciprocal.
traps.C: The reciprocal without the sign change.
traps.D: The gradient of the radius itself.
traps.E: Using the coordinates of the point rather than the differences.
traps.F: The y-coordinate of the centre.

questions.detail: Tangent gradient at a point on a circle

questions.stem_html:
In triangle ABC, angle A = 40°, a = 10 and b = 12.

How many distinct triangles satisfy this?
questions.solution_html:
By the sine rule, sin B = 12 sin 40°10 ≈ 0.771, so B ≈ 50.5° or 129.5°.

Both leave room for angle C: 40 + 50.5 < 180 and 40 + 129.5 < 180. So there are 2 triangles.

The obtuse option is only valid if the angles still sum to less than 180°. Here 169.5° leaves 10.5° for C — tight, but real.

traps.A: sin B < 1, so at least one triangle exists.
traps.B: The obtuse case also fits: 40° + 129.5° is still under 180°.
traps.D: The sine rule offers at most two values of B in range.
traps.E: Not reachable.
traps.F: Two sides and a non-included angle fix the triangle up to the ambiguity.

questions.stem_html:
A triangle has sides 5 and 7 with an angle of 60° between them.

What is its area?
questions.solution_html:
Area = 12ab sin C = 12 × 5 × 7 × sin 60°.

sin 60° = √32, so the area is 35√34.

The 60° is between the two given sides, so no cosine rule is needed — finding the third side first is a minute wasted.

traps.A: sin 60° replaced by 1/2.
traps.B: sin 45° used instead of sin 60°.
traps.C: The ½ ab product with sin 60° omitted entirely.
traps.E: The factor of ½ dropped.
traps.F: 5 × 7 — neither the half nor the sine applied.

questions.detail: Area from two sides and the angle between

questions.stem_html:
A sector of a circle has radius 6 and angle π3 radians.

What is the area of the segment cut off by the chord?
questions.solution_html:
Sector area = 12r2θ = 12 × 36 × π3 = 6π.

Triangle area = 12r2 sin θ = 18 × √32 = 9√3.

Segment = sector − triangle = 6π − 9√3.

The formula 12r2(θ − sin θ) does both steps at once, and only works in radians.

traps.A: Triangle area taken as ½r² without the sine.
traps.C: sin(π/3) read as 1/2 rather than √3/2.
traps.D: The sector area alone — the triangle not subtracted.
traps.E: Sector area doubled.
traps.F: ½r²θ computed with θ = π.

questions.stem_html: How many solutions does 2cos2x + cos x − 1 = 0 have for 0 ≤ x < 2π?
questions.solution_html:
Factorise in cos x: (2cos x − 1)(cos x + 1) = 0.

cos x = 12 gives x = π3 and 5π3. cos x = −1 gives x = π.

3 solutions in all.

cos x = −1 has only one solution in the interval, not two — the curve touches −1 rather than crossing it. Assuming every value of cos gives two solutions is what makes 4 so tempting.

traps.A: Only the cos x = −1 branch.
traps.B: Only the cos x = ½ branch.
traps.D: Assuming cos x = −1 gives two solutions; it gives one.
traps.E: Over-counting both branches.
traps.F: Three values of cos x with two solutions each — but there are only two values.

questions.detail: Counting solutions of a trig quadratic

questions.stem_html:
y = x3 + 2xx.

What is dydx when x = 3?
questions.solution_html:
Divide first: y = x2 + 2.

dydx = 2x, which at x = 3 is 6.

The quotient rule works and takes four lines. Dividing through takes one, and this is the whole reason the question is worth asking.

traps.A: The constant term, which differentiates to zero.
traps.B: The value of x, not the gradient.
traps.D: x² at x = 3 — the function, not its derivative.
traps.E: The value of y at x = 3.
traps.F: The numerator at x = 3, undivided.

questions.stem_html:
The normal to y = x2 at the point (1, 1) meets the curve again.

What is the x-coordinate of that second point?
questions.solution_html:
dydx = 2x = 2 at (1, 1), so the normal has gradient −12.

Normal: y = 1 − 12(x − 1). Setting y = x2:

x2 − 1 = −12(x − 1), and dividing by (x − 1) — valid for the other point — gives x + 1 = −12, so x = −32.

(x − 1) is a factor of both sides, because x = 1 is already known to be a solution. Cancelling it turns a quadratic into a linear equation.

traps.B: The reflection of x = 1, which is where the tangent would be parallel.
traps.C: The gradient of the normal, not an x-coordinate.
traps.D: Sign error after cancelling.
traps.E: The right magnitude with the sign lost.
traps.F: A guess at the far side of the curve.

questions.detail: Where a normal meets the curve again

questions.stem_html: For how many integer values of k does x3 − 3x + k = 0 have three distinct real roots?
questions.solution_html:
f(x) = x3 − 3x + k has turning points at x = ±1, with values k + 2 and k − 2.

Three distinct roots need those to straddle zero: (k+2)(k−2) < 0, that is −2 < k < 2.

The integers are −1, 0 and 1 — 3 of them.

k = ±2 gives a repeated root, not three distinct ones, so the endpoints are excluded. Including them gives 5.

traps.A: k = 0 alone gives three roots: x = 0 and ±√3.
traps.B: Only k = 0 counted.
traps.C: One of ±1 missed.
traps.E: One endpoint wrongly included.
traps.F: Both endpoints included; k = ±2 give repeated roots.

questions.stem_html: What is the area of the region between the curve y = 4 − x2, the x-axis, and the lines x = 0 and x = 2?
questions.solution_html:
∫02(4 − x2) dx = [4x − x33]02.

= 8 − 83 = 163.

The curve stays above the axis on [0, 2], touching it exactly at x = 2, so there is no sign change to worry about.

traps.A: The second term alone.
traps.B: The value of y at x = 0, not an area.
traps.D: A slip: 8 − 2 rather than 8 − 8/3.
traps.E: 8 − 4/3, from a slip evaluating x³/3 at x = 2 as 4/3 rather than 8/3.
traps.F: The 4x term alone, with the x³/3 forgotten.

questions.stem_html:
∫14f(x) dx = 10 and ∫12f(x) dx = 3.

What is ∫24f(x) dx?
questions.solution_html:
Integrals join end to end: ∫14 = ∫12 + ∫24.

So the answer is 10 − 3 = 7.

No function is given and none is needed. Anyone looking for f has misread the question.

traps.A: 3 − 10 — the subtraction the wrong way round.
traps.B: The sign of the known piece, negated.
traps.C: The piece that was given, not the one asked for.
traps.D: Dividing the integrals rather than subtracting.
traps.E: 10 + 3 — added instead of subtracted.

questions.stem_html:
The trapezium rule with two strips is used to estimate ∫02x2 dx.

What is the estimate, and how does it compare with the true value?
questions.solution_html:
With h = 1 and ordinates 0, 1, 4:

12 × 1 × [0 + 2(1) + 4] = 3.

The true value is 83 ≈ 2.67, so the estimate is an overestimate.

That is no accident: y = x2 is convex, so every chord lies above the curve and the trapezia always overshoot.

The direction of the error follows from the shape alone — convex means over, concave means under — so you can answer the second half without computing anything.

traps.A: The wrong estimate and, as it happens, the wrong direction too.
traps.C: The right estimate; the curve is convex, so the chords lie above it.
traps.D: That is the exact integral — the trapezium rule is not exact for a quadratic.
traps.E: 4 is the final ordinate, not the estimate.
traps.F: Wrong on both counts.

questions.detail: Is the trapezium rule over or under?

questions.stem_html:
dydx = 6x2, and y = 5 when x = 1.

What is y when x = 2?
questions.solution_html:
y = 2x3 + c. At (1, 5): 5 = 2 + c, so c = 3.

At x = 2: y = 16 + 3 = 19.

The constant is the question. Integrating and stopping at y = 2x3 gives 16, which is sitting in the options.

traps.A: c taken as −5.
traps.B: 2x³ − 3 — the sign of c reversed.
traps.C: 2x³ with the constant of integration omitted.
traps.D: A slip: 2(2)³ read as 14.
traps.E: 6x² evaluated at x = 2 and halved — the derivative, not y.
